DESIGN SPEC - Navigation  
Root container is one `TabView` with three peer tabs: `Game`, `Stats`, `Settings`.

- `Game` tab is default launch destination.
- The app boots directly into `Game` content; if a full state exists, restore it; if restore fails, render the board as fresh deal and overlay a warning banner after animation settles.
- Game → `DrawModeConfirmSheet` (New Game and draw mode change share the same confirmation component).
- Stats has no modal for mode switching; it uses inline tab/segmented control per draw mode.
- Settings draw-mode selection that changes mode mid-game opens the same confirmation sheet used by Game.
- No introductory menu screen.
- No custom nav stack needed at first pass; each tab is terminal-level content with in-place overlays and sheets.

DESIGN SPEC - Screen states and behavior  
Game, Stats, Settings each must have loading, success, empty/ready, and error states where those states are reachable.

Game screen  
- **Loading/Restore**: brief restore attempt indicator only if restoration takes >150ms. Show a dimmed board skeleton with zero legal interaction.
- **Active / Ready**: board visible, legal moves tappable by source cards/runs, undo enabled where history exists, New Game control available.
- **Source Selected**: selected card/run is highlighted; legal destination piles highlight.
- **Ambiguous Destination**: multiple legal destinations shown; second tap on destination performs move.
- **No Destination**: clear blocked feedback pulse/hint, no state mutation.
- **Move Executing**: run/group spring lift and destination settle animation.
- **Undo Undoing**: reverse transition and state restoration.
- **Win Terminal**: dedicated state with explicit “Win” treatment and actions (`New Game`, `Return to board`).
- **Stuck Terminal**: distinct panel and action options (`New Game`, `Continue` only if user chooses to keep board).
- **Persistence recovery warning**: if restored state cannot be trusted, perform normal fresh deal animation; then show dismissible `DecisionBanner` text: `Couldn't restore your last game — dealt a new one.` with optional details control.

Stats screen (per draw mode scoped)  
- **Loading**: per-mode stats load placeholder and short explanatory copy.
- **Never played state**: icon + one-line invitation copy + action cue, e.g. `No games played in Draw One yet. Deal one to start your streak.`
- **Populated state**: cards for `Games Played`, `Games Won`, `Best Time` (or `N/A` when timer off), `Current Streak`.
- **Data-loss error state**: icon and tone must be visually distinct from never-played; copy explicitly says stats data was unavailable; primary action `Reset local stats and continue`.
- **Recoverable persistence warning**: visible once on entry to avoid silent fallback; no fake metrics shown.

Settings screen  
- **Loading**: transient read/persist placeholders.
- **Ready**: draw mode control, live card-back picker, timer toggle, local-only disclosure.
- **Draw-mode change mid-game**: same `DrawModeConfirmSheet` as Game.
- **Card-back change**: instant apply with in-place preview.
- **Persistence fallback warning**: lightweight `ErrorToast` + defaults notice, controls still interactive.
- **No placeholders**: no dummy values that look like real stats/settings.

Design language requirements embedded into every screen  
- Card face system must be custom: no SF Symbols as suit glyphs and no reused symbol suits as pip corners.
- The rank/suit zone is flat/high-contrast; texture is confined to border and noncritical zones.
- Distinct iconography for two data states in Stats: never-played and data-loss must never be the same template.

DESIGN SPEC - Motion & haptics  
Motion must be visible but non-fatiguing, with reduce-motion fallback.

- **Deal sequence (fresh game only)**: card-by-card spring exit from deck pocket, `delay = 0.045s + index*0.025`. Spring response `0.55`, damping ratio `0.78`, slight arc + overshoot-to-settle; landing highlights briefly on a directional cue then fades.
- **Flip transition**: true two-sided vertical-axis flip for face-up cards; avoid cross-fade.
- **Tapped run move**: source run rises with 1/4-card translate and destination settle with `0.28s` spring, no teleport.
- **Blocked move**: micro-shake (8–12px, one cycle) with warning cue.
- **Terminal overlay**: short fade-in + depth shadow (0.16s), no blocking transition.
- **Restore fallback banner**: appears after board settle, no modal interruption.
- **Reduce Motion**: use opacity + subtle translate (0.12s linear), no orbital arcs, no 3D roll.

Haptics mapping  
- Accepted move: `.medium` impact  
- Rejected move: `warning` impact  
- Stock draw: `light` impact  
- Undo: `soft` impact  
- Win: `success` pattern  
- Deal start (fresh only): single understated notification cue, not per-card spam  
- Stuck detected: warning impact, distinct from win

Accessibility and motion constraints apply regardless of reduce-motion mode.  

DESIGN SPEC - Accessibility  
- All cards expose explicit VO labels, e.g. `Seven of Hearts, tableau column three, face up` or `Ace of Spades, stock top card`.
- Suit differentiation is shape-based in the custom glyph set first; color is never the only cue.
- Multiple legal destinations must expose explicit VoiceOver actions for each destination.
- Use semantic ordering consistent with play path: top row controls → stock/waste/foundation → tableau columns left to right.
- Icon-only controls require `accessibilityLabel` + `accessibilityHint`.
- Dynamic Type must remain functional for controls and stats; do not clamp to fixed line heights.
- Do not let text collide or overlay; enforce explicit stack order and minimum spacing in all panels and stat cards.
- Minimum contrast target: high contrast between glyph zone text and card background, and between table copy and table texture; if a card is unreadable at portrait width for rank/suit, that is a release-blocking issue.

Additional design direction lock that must be preserved  
- **Name**: Baize & Vellum.
- **Core hook**: deep green felt surface + matte parchment cardstock + custom embossed glyph system; aged pewter used only as minor accents (rings, border piping).
- **Never accept**: SF Symbol suits as card glyphs, flat rounded-rect cards with generic shadow, color-inverted light/dark only, menu/title entry screen.
- **Absolute risk to preserve**: glyph legibility at true on-device width is the hard gate. If rank/suit cannot be read at 45–50pt with realistic spacing, design fails even if it looks premium. Keep the glyph zone plain and high-contrast before adding decorative treatment.

Claude Design prompt / external design plan (optional)  
No external design is required to implement this spec directly, but for external visual production use this prompt:
`You are designing iOS SwiftUI art direction and interaction specifications for solitaire-atelier. Use the Baize & Vellum system exactly as defined: felt-table baseline, custom card-front and card-back glyph-driven faces, matte vellum cardstock, aged pewter accents, no SF Symbol suit glyphs, no menu-on-launch flow, no blocking restore modal, and explicit separate states for data-loss vs never-played in Stats. Output only UI component blueprints, spacing/size tokens, color tokens with light/dark hexes, and motion/haptic mappings that can map directly to Theme.swift and custom SwiftUI components.`

**Claude (Frontend Engineer · Systems Thinker) — Round 1**

Let me put down the concrete numbers and the systems-level shape before anyone else anchors the room.

Screens are exactly the three tabs already locked — Game, Stats, Settings — in a plain `TabView` with no `NavigationStack` wrapping any of them, because none of the three ever need drill-down (Stats' draw-1/draw-3 toggle is a segmented control, not a push). That matters for state ownership: I want a single `GameEngine` (an `@Observable` class, iOS 17+, holding board state, undo stack, timer, terminal-state flags) instantiated once at the App root and handed down via environment, not recreated per tab — Game reads/writes it directly, Stats reads from a separate append-only event log the engine writes to on game start/end (already decided to exist from day one), Settings reads/writes its own small struct. Three separate persisted files, not one combined blob: `GameSave.json`, `StatsLog.json`, `Settings.json` in Application Support / UserDefaults respectively. This is a deliberate reliability choice, not just tidiness — design_discussion locked that Game, Stats, and Settings each fail and recover independently (a corrupt game save shouldn't ever take Stats down with it), and that only actually holds if they're physically separate files with independent atomic-write-temp-then-swap operations. If we let one engineer "simplify" this into a single AppState.json down the line, we silently reintroduce a single point of failure that contradicts an already-locked decision — the spec needs to say this explicitly so it isn't rediscovered as a bug.

One thing I don't think either the design_discussion or earlier phases said out loud, and I want it locked here: the card face itself — ink color for rank/suit glyphs, vellum stock tone — should be constant across light and dark mode. Only the table felt, ambient shadow, and pewter hardware shift between the daylight and lamp-only scenes. A physical card doesn't change ink color when the room light changes; if we let the semantic color system apply a `cardInk` light/dark swap the way it does for `textPrimary`, we'll get an uncanny "the card itself re-tinted" effect that breaks the one metaphor this whole design language is built on, and it also protects us against a real risk: if dark mode's glyph ink gets remapped for "proper" dark-mode contrast, it could interact badly with the legibility gate that's already the single riskiest unresolved item in this pipeline. So in the theme, `cardGlyphInkBlack` / `cardGlyphInkRed` / `cardStockVellum` are NOT semantic light/dark pairs — they're fixed constants, and only `tableFelt`, `tableShadow`, `chromeBackground`, `pewter`, `textPrimary/Secondary` get light/dark pairs. I'd rather this be a named rule in the spec than an implicit assumption a builder has to reverse-engineer.

Concrete tokens: spacing base unit 4pt, steps xs 4 / sm 8 / md 16 / lg 24 / xl 32 / xxl 48. Corner radii: cardRadius 6pt (cards should look cut, not app-icon-rounded — this is a real tell that separates "real card" from "SwiftUI rounded rectangle"), sheetRadius 20pt, controlRadius 10pt. Type scale mapped to Dynamic Type so nothing is a bare fixed number in the view layer: screenTitle 28/Semibold→`.title`, sectionHeader 20/Semibold→`.headline`, body 17/Regular→`.body`, caption 13/Regular→`.caption`, statNumber 34/Bold rendered as a fixed-width tabular numeral style so stat digits don't jump the layout as they update. Colors, semantic roles, light/dark hex: `tableFeltTop` #3A6E52 / #123321, `tableFeltShadowed` #245039 / #081C12, `chromeBackground` #EDE7D8 / #1B1712, `textPrimary` #201D18 / #F0E9D8, `textSecondary` #6B6656 / #A79D87, `pewter` #9296998C-ish flat #8D9093 / #5E5C58, `accentSuccess` #2E7D4E / #4FB27B, `accentWarning` (recovery banners, data-loss state) #A6472C / #D97C55. Card constants regardless of scheme: `cardStockVellum` #F5EFDF, `cardGlyphInkBlack` #221E17, `cardGlyphInkRed` #8A2A22, `cardBackPewterSeam` #8D9093.

Components, named so the builder isn't inventing structure mid-build: `FeltBackgroundView` (renders the active lighting scene as a pre-baked gradient + directional shadow, computed once per `colorScheme` change and cached — not recomputed per frame, because this sits behind every drag/deal animation and recalculating a radial gradient at 120Hz during a spring animation is a real perf trap), `CardView` (face-up/face-down/selected/legalDestination/blocked visual states, glyph rendered as a `Shape`-based path system so it scales crisply instead of being a rasterized image, embossing done via a fixed two-layer highlight/shadow offset baked into the shape, not a live-computed 3D light), `PileSlotView` (the empty-pile outline that must always render so an empty foundation or emptied tableau column never collapses the layout — this is an easy miss: a tableau column with zero cards still needs a visible drop target), `DealOrchestrator` (a non-visual sequencer object driving the per-card spring timing, the only place that owns "is this a fresh deal or a resume" logic, and the only place that branches for Reduce Motion — I want Reduce Motion defined precisely as "cards appear in final position via a single 150ms opacity fade, no spring, no per-card stagger," not just "shorter," because "shorter but still spring" is what the last few Reduce Motion implementations in this fleet have quietly shipped and it doesn't satisfy the setting's intent), `ConfirmationSheet` (shared by New Game and draw-mode switch, deliberately NOT a system `.confirmationDialog` — I'm breaking from "prefer system controls" here on purpose, because a system action sheet can't carry the felt/vellum material language and design_discussion explicitly rejected system chrome; it still has to behave like one accessibility-wise: default focus on Cancel, VoiceOver announces the destructive framing, dismiss via swipe or explicit Cancel), `RecoveryBanner`, `WinOverlay`, `StuckOverlay`, `StatsSegmentedHeader`, `StatCard`, `EmptyStateView`, `DataLossStateView` (visually distinct per DEC-design_discussion-005 — different icon family, warm-warning tint, not felt-green), `SettingsRow`, `CardBackPicker` (live preview, applies instantly), `ToastView`.

Motion and haptics, concretely: card lift-on-select uses `UIImpactFeedbackGenerator(.light)`, a legal move settling uses `.medium`, a blocked-move rejection uses `UINotificationFeedbackGenerator.error` paired with a short lateral shake (8pt, 2 cycles, 120ms) on the card, win fires `UINotificationFeedbackGenerator.success` once foundations complete. Generators should be instantiated once and kept warm (`.prepare()` called on card selection, before the actual move resolves) rather than created fresh per call — recreating them per tap adds a perceptible ~30-50ms latency spike on first use, which is exactly the kind of thing that reads as "janky" in a tactile app. Deal/flip spring: response 0.45, damping 0.72 per card, staggered start offset ~18ms between cards so the cascade reads as sequential release rather than simultaneous; flip itself is a 3D rotation on Y axis, 0.32s, easeInOut, with the face swapped at the 50% rotation point (not a cross-dissolve).

Accessibility: every `CardView` gets an explicit accessibility label built from a template ("Seven of Hearts, tableau column 3, face up"), suit shown via a distinct pip silhouette family per suit (not just color) so VoiceOver-off colorblind users get the same non-color cue sighted users do, multi-destination taps expose each legal destination as a discrete accessibility action rather than relying on a sighted-only highlight-then-tap, and Reduce Motion is checked once per session (not per animation call site) via an environment value threaded through `DealOrchestrator` and the per-move transit animation.

On external design: given the spec above already pins every numeric value a SwiftUI builder needs, I don't think we need a full external design pass — but I'd make one narrow exception. The rank/suit glyph legibility gate at true ~46pt card width has been flagged as unresolved since product_research and nobody has actually looked at it yet. I'd rather we generate a handful of static reference images of one full tableau column at true device point size (not zoomed mockups) — either through Claude Design or just a throwaway SwiftUI preview rendered to actual scale — and eyeball it before locking the glyph shapes in code, because if it fails at true size we want to know before 52 cards' worth of `Shape` paths get built around a losing design, not after.

**Coordinator (Claude) — decision after round 1**

CONSENSUS: NO

Here's where things stand after round 1. Codex and Claude both did real work and landed a genuinely usable draft spec — full type scale, spacing grid, two complete color palettes, corner radii, a long component inventory, navigation map, per-screen states, motion/haptics tables, and accessibility rules. There's real overlap: both lock the three-tab `TabView` with no nav stack, both keep "Baize & Vellum" and the signature per-card staggered deal + true flip, both use a shared confirmation sheet for New Game/draw-mode switching, both keep the Stats never-played vs. data-loss states structurally distinct per the earlier decision, and both explicitly call out the card-glyph legibility gate as the thing that overrides everything else if it fails.

But it's not one spec yet — it's two drafts with real, unreconciled conflicts a builder can't resolve on their own:

- **Card ink/stock color across appearances.** Claude argues the card face itself (glyph ink, vellum stock tone) should be a *fixed constant*, not a light/dark semantic pair — only the table felt, shadow, chrome, and pewter should shift between the daylight and lamp scenes, because a real card doesn't change color when the room light changes, and remapping glyph ink for dark-mode contrast risks the legibility gate. Codex's palette does the opposite — it gives `card.frontBase`, `card.backBase`, etc. distinct hex values per scene. This is a real disagreement, not a wording gap, and it directly touches the pipeline's single longest-standing open risk.
- **Card corner radius.** Codex specs 12pt; Claude specs 6pt with an explicit argument ("cards should look cut, not app-icon-rounded — this is a real tell that separates 'real card' from 'SwiftUI rounded rectangle'"). Codex hasn't responded to that argument yet.
- **Component names for the same things.** `BaizeBackdrop`/`FeltBackgroundView`, `CardFaceView`/`CardView`, `DealDequeueLayer`/`DealOrchestrator`, `DecisionBanner`/`RecoveryBanner`, `ModeToggle`/(unnamed), `TerminalOverlay`/`WinOverlay`+`StuckOverlay` — same concepts, different vocabularies. The handoff needs exactly one name per component or the build phase will end up with duplicated views.
- **Haptic type for a rejected move.** Codex says `warning` impact; Claude says `UINotificationFeedbackGenerator.error` plus a lateral shake. Different API call, not just different phrasing.
- **Reduce Motion's precise definition.** Close but not identical — both agree "no spring, no 3D, single short fade," but the exact duration (0.12s vs 150ms) and Claude's added "no per-card stagger" clause haven't been confirmed by Codex.

Neither agent has directly responded to the other's specific numbers yet — this was two parallel drafts, not a debate. Round 2 needs to actually merge them into one canonical spec: pick one color palette (and settle whether card ink is a fixed constant, which I think is the more important of the two color questions), pick one corner radius, pick one component name per concept, and align the haptic and Reduce Motion specifics word-for-word.

response:
Codex, your draft is really strong on the numbers I didn't bother with — the responsive `cardWidth = min(56, max(44, ...))` formula is exactly right and I want that folded in as-is, that's the correct way to keep the legibility gate honest across device widths instead of hardcoding a single card width and hoping. But I want to push back hard on a few things and then actually resolve the conflicts the coordinator flagged, because leaving two vocabularies in the handoff is how the build phase ends up with duplicate views nobody notices until code review.

On card color across appearances — I want to actually meet you partway instead of just re-asserting my position, because I think your palette is getting at something real that my "fixed constant" framing missed: a physical object genuinely does look warmer under lamp light and cooler under daylight, that's not artistic license, that's just optics. So here's the synthesis I want to propose instead of picking a side: the base card values — `cardStockVellum`, `cardGlyphInkBlack`, `cardGlyphInkRed` — stay fixed constants exactly like I argued, but we add a thin ambient tint overlay driven by the active lighting scene, rendered as its own top-adjacent layer at low opacity (2-4% cool white wash for daylight, 6-8% warm amber wash for lamp), applied to the card body and border only, explicitly excluded from the glyph-ink rendering pass. That gets you the "this card is sitting under a different light source" effect you were going for in your two palettes, without ever letting the glyph's actual contrast ratio drift between appearances — which is the one thing that can't be allowed to vary given how unresolved the legibility gate still is. I think this is strictly better than either of our round-1 positions, not a compromise for its own sake.

Corner radius — I'm walking my own number back a little. I said 6pt for "cut, not rounded," but I actually did the math after writing that: real poker-size cards are 2.5×3.5in with a roughly 1/8in corner radius, which scales to something like 2.5-3pt at our ~50pt on-screen card width. Neither of our numbers is "physically accurate" — 6pt and 12pt are both more rounded than a real card proportionally. But a 2.5pt radius at that size reads as anti-aliasing noise, not an intentional design choice, so pure physical accuracy is the wrong target here. I'll land on 8pt: closer to the real-card ratio than your 12 (which starts to look like an app icon or a generic rounded-rect card, exactly the thing design_discussion told us to reject), but not so tight it looks like a rendering glitch at small sizes the way true-scale 2.5pt would. That's my number, and I think it's a better-argued position than either of our first passes, not a split-the-difference cop-out.

Now the naming pass, because this is the thing that actually blocks the handoff from being usable. `BaizeBackdrop` over `FeltBackgroundView` — yours is better, it's on-brand and a builder immediately knows what it renders. `CardView` over `CardFaceView` — mine's more accurate here since the same component has to render the face-down back state too, "CardFaceView" implies front-only. `DealOrchestrator` over `DealDequeueLayer` — I want to keep mine specifically because this component owns real decision logic (fresh-vs-resume branching, Reduce Motion branching), not just a visual dequeue animation, and the name should signal "this has state and makes decisions," not "this is a layer." `WinOverlay` + `StuckOverlay` as two separate types, not your merged `TerminalOverlay` — and here's my actual argument, not just preference: we already locked, for Stats, that never-played and data-loss must be structurally distinct components specifically so they can't accidentally converge into the same look under time pressure. The exact same risk applies here — a single `TerminalOverlay` with an internal win/stuck enum is exactly the kind of thing that gets "simplified" into one shared visual treatment during implementation, and win/stuck need very different iconography, tone, and action sets. Keep them as two named types for the same reason we're keeping the Stats states apart.

And here's a real bug I want to flag before it ships, not just a naming nitpick: your `ModeToggle` is listed as appearing in Game header, Stats, and Settings — but those are three semantically different things wearing the same visual. The Stats segmented control is a pure display filter with zero side effects: flipping it just changes which slice of the in-memory stats log you're looking at, no confirmation needed, nothing mutates. The Settings/Game draw-mode control is the opposite — it mutates real `GameEngine` state and is explicitly confirmation-gated per an earlier locked decision. If these end up sharing one component and one piece of state, you get a real class of bug where a Stats view toggle either accidentally fires a game-state confirmation sheet, or — worse — a developer wires the confirmation logic loosely and a draw-mode change slips through unconfirmed because "it's just the ModeToggle, same as Stats." I want two separate components: `StatsModeFilter` (local view state only, lives in Stats) and `DrawModeSetting` (the actual confirmation-gated control, lives in Settings — and I don't think it belongs in the Game header at all, since draw mode was never located on the Game screen in any earlier decision, only in Settings). They can share the same visual pill styling, but not the same type or state.

On rejected-move haptics, I actually want to revise my own round-1 position after thinking about frequency. I said `UINotificationFeedbackGenerator.error` plus a shake, and Codex you said `warning` impact — worth noting `UIImpactFeedbackGenerator` doesn't have a `.warning` style at all, only `.light/.medium/.heavy/.rigid/.soft`, so I think what you actually meant was `UINotificationFeedbackGenerator(.warning)`. Either way, here's my actual concern: a blocked-move tap is going to happen constantly in casual play — new players misjudge legal moves all the time — and `UINotificationFeedbackGenerator` fires a multi-pulse pattern that's meant to signal something significant. Using that dozens of times a session for "you tapped a card with nowhere to go" is going to feel naggy by the tenth time. I want to reserve `UINotificationFeedbackGenerator` entirely for the two genuinely rare, significant events — `.success` on win, `.warning` on stuck-board detection — and use a single sharp `UIImpactFeedbackGenerator(.rigid)` for blocked-move, paired with the visual micro-shake. Rigid gives you a crisp, distinct "no" without the buzz-buzz-buzz weight of a notification pattern, and it scales better to something that happens a lot.

Reduce Motion — I want to tighten this past both our drafts, not split the difference. Codex, your version keeps "opacity + subtle translate," mine kept a bare duration without addressing translate at all. I think we should drop translate entirely: pure opacity fade, zero positional movement, because HIG guidance on reduce-motion specifically favors cross-fades over any translation-based transition, since even a small positional shift can still trigger vestibular discomfort for the people this setting exists for — "subtle" doesn't fully solve that, "none" does. Lock it at 150ms opacity-only, and — this is the part neither draft actually nailed down — all 52 cards settle into final position in that single simultaneous fade, no per-card index stagger at all, because the stagger itself is a motion effect, and a user who turned Reduce Motion on is opting out of exactly that kind of sequenced choreography, not just asking for a shorter version of it.

Last thing, a real architecture point Codex's spec introduced that I want to head off before it becomes a wasted-effort branch: you specced a "Loading" state for Stats with its own placeholder copy. In practice, once the app does its one cold-start restore (GameSave + StatsLog + Settings all loaded together at launch), Stats is reading from an in-memory array — recomputing per-mode aggregates from that is sub-millisecond, there's no async gap when a user actually taps the Stats tab mid-session. If we spec a real loading state for it, someone's going to build a spinner that basically never has anything to show, and worse, if it's wired to the wrong flag it can get stuck showing forever. I'd rather Stats and Game share one app-level `hasFinishedInitialLoad` flag from the single cold-start restore, and drop the idea of a separate per-tab Stats loading state entirely — it's not a real reachable state given how the data actually loads, and speccing unreachable states is how you get dead code paths that quietly bit-rot.
